H&P – Super Detailed

Consult Summary:
28-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presents with a first-time, severe (8/10) left occipital headache of 1-day duration, without red-flag features; advised stepped-up analgesia, hydration, rest, and safety-net follow-up.

History:
• Presenting complaint: New headache.  
• Onset: Began yesterday mid-morning.  
• Location: Left posterior (occipital) head.  
• Quality: Intense, throbbing; built up gradually over a short period.  
• Severity: 8/10 pain scale.  
• Temporal profile: Continuous since onset; no particular time-of-day variation.  
• Provoking/relieving: Not affected by position (lying, standing, bending, cough, sneeze). Ibuprofen yesterday provided no relief.  
• Associated symptoms: Denies nausea, vomiting, visual changes, photophobia, aura, tingling, numbness, weakness, fever, chills, sweats, rash, neck stiffness.  
• Functional impact: Finding it hard to perform work-related and normal activities.  
• Previous headaches: None.  
• Systems review: Otherwise eating and drinking normally; no systemic or neurological symptoms reported.  

Past Medical History:
• No chronic medical conditions reported.  
• No prior headaches.  

Medications:
• Ibuprofen (Nurofen) yesterday – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• No regular prescription or OTC medications.  

Allergies:
• No drug or food allergies reported.

Social History:
• Lives with partner.  
• Occupation: Designer; has not yet missed work but finding tasks difficult.  
• Tobacco: Never smoker.  
• Alcohol: Denies regular use.  
• Recreational drugs: Denies use.  

Family History:
• Mother: Hypertension; migraines.  
• No other familial illnesses mentioned.

Physical Examination:
• No in-consultation physical exam performed (remote video call).  
• Vitals not available.

Investigations:
• None performed or available at time of consult.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Acute unilateral (left occipital) headache, first episode, no red-flag features identified
  • Assessment: Severe (8/10) new-onset headache without focal neurology or systemic signs. Differential includes tension-type, early migraine, medication-nonresponsive primary headache; low suspicion for secondary causes given absence of red flags but to monitor.  
  • Plan:
    – Trial stronger NSAID (name/dose not documented) in place of ibuprofen; take regularly with food.  
    – May use paracetamol concurrently.  
    – Encourage rest and adequate hydration.  
    – Safety-net: Seek medical review if headache worsens, fails to improve within 1–2 days, or if new symptoms develop (fever, rash, vomiting, neck stiffness, visual changes, neurological deficits, recurrent episodes).  
    – Consider in-person evaluation including blood pressure measurement and neurological examination if symptoms persist.  
    – Follow-up: Telephone or in-person review if not settling in 24–48 h.  

General plan items:
• Pharmacist prescription to be issued for stronger NSAID (details not documented).  
• Educated patient on medication timing and not to overlap NSAIDs.  

Quality checks:

Missing but clinically expected:
• Vital signs and focused neurological examination.  
• Exact name/dose/frequency of newly recommended NSAID.  
• Detailed allergy confirmation (listed as none but not specifically asked about non-drug allergies).  
• Medication reconciliation (OTC/herbal supplements).  

Internal conflicts:
• None noted.  

Transcript quality:
• Clear audio; no significant inaudible sections.
